title: Röntgen discovers X-rays
summary: On the evening of 8 November 1895 at the University of Würzburg, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen found that a plate coated with barium platinocyanide glowed even when his discharge tube was sealed in thick black carton. He called the unknown radiation X-rays, and his image of his wife's hand showed the shadows of her bones and ring. He received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

as_recorded.value: On the evening of November 8, 1895, he found that, if the discharge tube is enclosed in a sealed, thick black carton to exclude all light, and if he worked in a dark room, a paper plate covered on one side with barium platinocyanide placed in the path of the rays became fluorescent
On Friday, November 8, 1895 late in the afternoon Röntgen set up some experiments on cathode rays in his laboratory at the University of Würzburg

where.modern_name: Röntgen Memorial, Röntgenring 8a, Würzburg, Bavaria, Germany
where.historical_name: Physics Institute, University of Würzburg, German Empire

importance.justification: Gave science and medicine a way to see inside solid bodies, and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

sources.title: Claims of priority - The scientific path to the discovery of X-rays

reviewer_note: Röntgen is the accepted discoverer, but the Busch review sets out earlier observations and rival claims of priority. The pin is the Röntgen memorial at Röntgenring 8a, Würzburg.
